Congressional Research Service                                                                    203

## Page 208

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



For REAP, H.R. 7567 would amend the selection criteria to receive a grant to include “the
potential of the proposed program to meaningfully improve the financial conditions of the
agricultural producer or rural small business” and the award considerations to receive a loan
guarantee or a grant to include “the potential improvements to the financial conditions of the
agricultural producer or rural small business.” S. 5526 would expand the program to include the
provision of technical assistance to those applying for financial assistance, addition of an
“agricultural producer cooperative” as an eligible entity, requirement for the Secretary to establish
a simplified application process for projects requesting less than $50,000, and increase of the
percentage of funding the Secretary may issue for grants for lower-cost activities (i.e., activities
that cost $50,000 or less). S. 5526 would also establish a rebate pilot project for eligible entities
for the purchase of certain energy-efficient equipment.

H.R. 7567 would add two new sections to the energy title pertaining to solar energy. Section 9011
would require USDA to conduct a study on the effects of solar panel installations on the
conversion of certain farmland out of agricultural production. USDA would be required to (1)
analyze the economic effects of solar panel installations on certain farmland; (2) investigate the
impacts of solar panel installation, operation, and decommissioning on certain farmland; (3)
assess the impacts of shared solar energy and agricultural production on certain farmland; and (4)
assess the “types of agricultural lands best suited and worst suited for shared solar energy and
agricultural production.” USDA would be required to consult with the Department of Energy and
relevant stakeholders while conducting the study. USDA would be required to submit to the
House Committee on Agriculture, the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the Senate
Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, and the Senate Committee on Energy and
Natural Resources a written report on the study findings and recommendations. Section 9012
would prohibit USDA from providing financial assistance for a project that would result in the
conversion of certain farmland for solar energy production. Exceptions to this prohibition would
include projects converting less than five acres of certain farmland, generally, and projects
converting less than 50 acres with the majority of the energy produced used for on-farm use and
receiving approval or support from the county and municipality where the project is located. The
bill would prohibit USDA from providing financial assistance for projects that procure solar
energy components produced, manufactured, or assembled in a foreign country of concern; by an
entity domiciled or controlled by a foreign country of concern; or by a foreign entity of concern
as defined by 42 U.S.C. §19237. S. 5526 does not include provisions pertaining to solar energy,
including new programs.
H.R. 7567 would support the development of SAF.67 It would modify the definition of advanced
biofuel (7 U.S.C. §8101(3)(B)) to include SAF. It would require USDA to establish a department-
wide strategy to advance the production of SAF that would (1) facilitate collaboration between
relevant mission areas to encourage the advancement of the SAF supply chain; (2) identify
opportunities to maximize SAF development, deployment, and commercialization; (3) leverage
the capabilities of U.S. farmers and others to capture opportunities in the SAF market; (4) support
rural economic development through SAF production; and (5) promote public-private
partnerships for the development, deployment, and commercialization of SAF. S. 5526 contains
identical provisions that would support the development of SAF.

Additionally, H.R. 7567 would raise awareness regarding agricultural irrigation pumping systems.
The bill would require USDA to make available to the public information about cost savings and
energy savings that can be realized with the use of energy-efficient pumping systems. It also
would require USDA to develop an energy efficiency preassessment tool for pumping systems

## Page 217

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



Title X, Horticulture, Marketing, and Regulatory Reform68

The respective horticulture, marketing, and regulatory reform titles of H.R. 7567, as passed by the
House, and of S. 5526, as reported by the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and
Forestry, would reauthorize and amend many of the 2018 farm bill provisions and programs
relating to the specialty crop sector, certified organic agriculture, local and urban food systems,
hemp production, pesticide use, and other marketing and regulatory efforts (Table 13).

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would reauthorize USDA to issue block grants to states through FY2031
to enhance the competitiveness of specialty crops and amend the purpose of the grants to reflect
state priorities and input from stakeholders. The bills also would reauthorize appropriations for
programs such as Specialty Crops Market News and the Acer Access and Development Program.
H.R. 7567 would reauthorize appropriations at current levels for the National Organic Program
(NOP) through FY2031, while S. 5526 would increase the levels of authorized appropriations for
the NOP for the same period. In addition, both bills would expand the mission and responsibilities
of the Office of Urban Agriculture and Innovative Production.

H.R. 7567 would amend the domestic hemp production program to reflect changes to the
statutory definition of hemp that were made in P.L. 119-37.69 The bill would relax certain
requirements for producers of industrial hemp, including by reducing or eliminating testing
requirements and by taking steps to eliminate the existing 10-year period of ineligibility
following the date of conviction for a controlled substance-related felony. Additionally, the bill
would require USDA to establish a process to accredit laboratories for testing hemp in
consultation with the Drug Enforcement Administration. S. 5526 contains no amendments to the
statutes that govern hemp.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would extend the authority of USDA to issue grants to local and regional
producers through the Local Agriculture Market Program (LAMP) until FY2031, expand the list
of businesses eligible for grant funding in LAMP, expand the purposes of grant funding, and
require USDA to seek input from stakeholders on a simplified application and reporting process.
H.R. 7567 differs from S. 5526 in that it would expand eligible activities for LAMP grants to
include the purchase of special purpose equipment and other activities.

Both H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would make amendments to the NOP. The similar amendments in
both bills include authorizing USDA to offer technical assistance to organic producers; defining
“risk to organic integrity” and “oversight protocols”; and requiring USDA to conduct a study on
whether oversight protocols based on the risk to organic integrity may lead to additional NOP
regulations. While both bills allow for changes to inspection protocols for operations that pose a
lower risk to organic integrity, such as allowing virtual inspections for some operations, S. 5526
would make these allowances conditional on the results of the study. H.R. 7567 contains some
organic provisions that are not in S. 5526, such as a proposal to require USDA to collect and
publish cost-of-production data for organic milk. Additionally, H.R. 7567 would extend the
requirement for USDA to submit an annual report to Congress on enforcement and compliance
actions in NOP through March 1, 2031.

## Page 218

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 contain comparable provisions that would amend the Federal Insecticide,
Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA; 7 U.S.C. §§136 et seq.) for various purposes, including
to exclude certain plant biostimulants from the statute and exempt certain plant-incorporated
protectants from the requirements of the statute. These bills would provide for additional
coordination among the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and other federal agencies on
the implementation of FIFRA, including the evaluation of pesticide registrations and their
potential effects on listed species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA; 16 U.S.C.
§§1531 et seq.). Both bills would extend the deadline until October 2031 for initial registration
reviews of pesticides registered prior to October 2016 that have not undergone initial registration
reviews. Unlike H.R.7567, S. 5526 would require USDA to conduct a study and report on the
types and use of biostimulants to achieve specified nutrient management, environmental, and
agricultural objectives.

S. 5526 contains provisions, some of which are related to plant pest and disease management, that
have no comparable provisions in the House-passed bill. These include provisions that would (1)
expand inspection services for which USDA employees can be paid to include interstate
movement of products between the continental United States and Alaska and Hawaii and (2)
authorize USDA to use appropriated funds for the construction and operation of research
laboratories, quarantine stations, and related facilities.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would establish an Office of Biotechnology Policy (OBP) within USDA.
Both bills would require OBP to provide leadership for interagency coordination with EPA, the
Food and Drug Administration, and other federal and state agencies. H.R. 7567 would establish
OBP to coordinate department policies and activities relating to biotechnology, biomanufacturing,
synthetic biology, and other emerging technologies, including research, extension, and education;
communication, regulation, and labeling; and commercialization. H.R. 7567 would have OBP
oversee policy coordination across research, cooperative extension, communication, regulation,
and commercialization. S. 5526 would establish OBP under a different statutory authority and
state that its purpose is to coordinate agricultural policies and activities concerning biotechnology,
biomanufacturing, and related topics. It would explicitly assign OBP responsibility for
coordinating biotechnology activities carried out under specified USDA authorities and in
consultation with USDA agencies on biotechnology responsibilities under FIFRA; the Federal
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act; Food Quality Protection Act of 1996; and other applicable laws.

## Page 232

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



Title XI, Crop Insurance70

The Federal Crop Insurance Program (FCIP) offers subsidized crop insurance policies that
producers can purchase to insure a wide variety of crops and livestock. Policies pay indemnities
for yield and revenue losses due to adverse growing and market conditions, including natural
disasters. The Federal Crop Insurance Corporation (FCIC), a government corporation within
USDA, pays part of the premium (about 61% on average in crop year 2025) and policyholders—
farmers and ranchers—pay the balance. Private insurance companies, known as Approved
Insurance Providers (AIPs), sell and service the policies in return for administrative and operating
(A&O) subsidies from the FCIC. The FCIC also reinsures a portion of the AIPs’ underwriting risk
as specified in a mutually negotiated Standard Reinsurance Agreement. The USDA Risk
Management Agency administers the FCIP. The FCIP is permanently authorized under the
Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 (P.L. 75-430, 52 Stat. 72) and the Federal Crop Insurance
Act of 1980 (P.L. 96-365, 7 U.S.C. §§1501 et seq.), as amended. Congress recently made changes
to the FCIP in the FY2025 budget reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21) to increase various premium
and A&O subsidies, modify certain insurance policies, and increase funds available for program
compliance and integrity.71 The respective crop insurance titles of H.R. 7567, as passed by the
House, and of S. 5526, as reported by the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and
Forestry, would make multiple changes to the program with implications for policyholders, AIPs,
and USDA (Table 14).

Implications for Policyholders

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would modify the definition of veteran farmers and ranchers used in the
FCIP and increase premium subsidies available for these individuals.72 These changes would
grant qualified veteran farmers and ranchers the same set of FCIP benefits that are available for
beginning farmers and ranchers. Both bills would exempt some individuals from beneficial
ownership interest reporting requirements.

Implications for Approved Insurance Providers

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would impose new requirements on AIPs and grant AIPs additional
recourse from notification requirements for compliance problems. Both bills would amend the
requirements for final agency determinations. H.R. 7567 would specify that the requirement for
the FCIC to establish procedures applies only to binding final agency determinations. S. 5526
would grant the FCIC exclusive authority to interpret crop insurance regulations and prohibit
judicial review of final agency determinations. S. 5526 would allow all program participants to
request FCIC interpretations and establish certain requirements for FCIC procedures for final
agency determinations. Additionally, S. 5526 would apply and bind FCIC final agency
determinations on all program participants, the National Appeals Division, and all courts of
competent jurisdiction.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would remove the limit on the maximum A&O subsidy rate that USDA
could assign to policies created after 2026 and require USDA to maintain A&O subsidy rates for

Congressional Research Service                                                                    228

## Page 233

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



policies created prior to 2027 at the rates in effect for the 2026 reinsurance year. H.R. 7567 would
authorize AIPs to charge certain late fees to delinquent policyholders; S. 5526 would not make
changes to the late fee policy.

Implications for USDA

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would retain the prohibition on the simultaneous purchase of a Stacked
Income Protection Plan policy and enrollment in either Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) or
Price Loss Coverage (PLC) programs and would shift these prohibitions from the parts of the
U.S. Code authorizing the FCIP to the parts of the U.S. Code authorizing the ARC and PLC
programs.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would specify the FCIC’s authority to provide yield and revenue
coverage. Both bills would require USDA to study and report on modifications to reinsurance
funds and crop insurance compensation, to reevaluate the Whole Farm Revenue Protection
coverage available for certain commodities, and to periodically review quality loss adjustment
procedures. H.R. 7567 would not make changes to crop insurance options that exclude certain
years from a producer’s production history calculations. S. 5526 would require the FCIC to
exclude yields from production history calculations for producers who were adversely impacted
by the Fargo-Moorhead metropolitan area flood risk management project.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would establish a specialty crop advisory committee. H.R. 7567 would
remove the requirement for the FCIC Board to include at least one specialty crop producer and
add a requirement for the FCIC Board to include at least one livestock producer. S. 5526 would
require the FCIC Board to include at least one specialty crop producer, at least one crop and
livestock producer, and at least one underserved producer who is a beginning farmer or rancher.
S. 5526 would also increase the quorum for the FCIC Board from four to six members. H.R. 7567
would not create a statutory definition of specialty crops for the purposes of the FCIP. S. 5526
would create a statutory definition of specialty crops that aligns with the statutory definition used
in other USDA programs.
H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would modify certain rules that apply to private sector submissions.73 H.R.
7567 would require USDA to periodically evaluate the actuarial performance of FCIP insurance
products developed by the private sector, impose certain requirements on the FCIC concerning
private sector submissions, and permit submissions of products developed by the private sector
without letters of support from an AIP. S. 5526 would not make these changes and would prohibit
the FCIC from requiring an AIP to appear in person when the AIP is assisting an applicant with an
in-person presentation.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would require USDA to conduct a pilot project to study the effects of late
planting on irrigation water use in the Ogallala Aquifer. Both bills would require USDA to
conduct research to develop coverage options for new priority areas, with some differences in
priority areas between the bills. Both bills would require USDA to study and report on
modifications to crop insurance and commodity support programs that would enhance risk
management options for lamb producers. H.R. 7567 would require USDA to study and report on
the effects of weather station outages on hurricane insurance coverage and changes to Livestock
Revenue Protection policies for feeder cattle impacted by natural disasters; S. 5526 does not
include these requirements.



73 The private sector can propose new types of FCIP policies and coverages as authorized under 7 U.S.C. §1508(h);
these are often referred to as “508(h) submissions.” For additional background, see CRS Report R46686, Federal Crop
Insurance: A Primer, by Stephanie Rosch.

## Page 241

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



Title XII, Miscellaneous74

The respective miscellaneous titles of H.R. 7567, as passed by the House, and of S. 5526, as
reported by the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, cover a variety of
provisions across five subtitles. Both bills would extend authorization of appropriations for some
programs through FY2031 and reauthorize certain provisions of the U.S. Grain Standards Act
(USGSA; P.L. 64-190; 39 Stat. 482; 7 U.S.C. §§71 et seq.) through FY2033 (Table 15).

Livestock and Other Animals

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would require USDA to evaluate the Cattle Fever Tick Eradication
Program and to submit a report on USDA support for livestock and poultry operations during
animal disease outbreaks to the agriculture committees of jurisdiction.75 Both bills would
authorize USDA to establish additional National Detector Dog Training Centers with off-site state
partnerships and strategic site considerations and to set dog importation requirements. S. 5526
would authorize appropriations of $15 million annually through FY2031 for the dog training
centers. H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would allow livestock marketing agencies to hold an ownership
interest in meat processing facilities. The bills would require USDA to provide guidance on
Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point plans to small and very small meat processors and to
conduct outreach for the Food Safety and Inspection Service Cooperative Interstate Shipping
Program.76

H.R. 7567 would restrict a state from enacting and enforcing production standards on livestock
products not produced in the state. H.R. 7567 would amend animal welfare provisions, such as by
establishing requirements for the importation of dogs, requiring federal research facilities to
facilitate the adoption or non-laboratory placement of certain animals no longer needed for
research, and prohibiting certain commercial greyhound racing activities. H.R. 7567 would
establish a pilot program to allow custom slaughter facilities that are exempt from inspection to
sell meat and poultry products directly to consumers. S. 5526 does not include those provisions.

S. 5526 would codify the National Poultry Improvement Plans and the U.S. Swine Health
Improvement Plan, exempt interstate internet sales of certain state-inspected meat and poultry
from certain federal inspections, and require USDA to submit a report to the agriculture
committees of jurisdiction on meat-packer concentration.

Department of Agriculture Reorganization Act of 1994

H.R. 7567 would amend various authorities of several USDA entities in the Department of
Agriculture Reorganization Act of 1994 (1994 USDA Reorganization Act; Title II of P.L. 103-
354), including the Office of Homeland Security, the Office of Tribal Relations, and the National
Appeals Division.77 S. 5526 would not amend authorities of the Office of Tribal Relations or the
National Appeals Division. H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would expand the duties of the Office of
Homeland Security and create an Office of Seafood.

National Security

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would amend the Agricultural Foreign Investment Disclosure Act of 1978
(AFIDA; P.L. 95-460). H.R. 7567 proposes amendments to Committee on Foreign Investment in
the United States (CFIUS) authorities and provisions relating to restricting foreign adversaries
from ownership of U.S. agricultural land. H.R. 7567 would require USDA to provide information
on foreign ownership of agricultural land to CFIUS, create an office to monitor AFIDA
compliance, provide annual reports to certain committees of Congress on agricultural land
purchasing activities, update the AFIDA handbook, and establish an electronic database of land
registrations by foreign owners.78 H.R. 7567 would amend CFIUS authorities under Section 721
of the Defense Production Act of 1950 (50 U.S.C. §4565) to add the Secretary of Agriculture as a
CFIUS member with respect to certain types of foreign investment transactions involving
agriculture and to require CFIUS to consider for review “reportable agricultural land
transactions” as notified to CFIUS by the Secretary of Agriculture.79 H.R. 7567 would require the
President to direct the heads of federal departments and agencies to promulgate rules and
regulations that would prohibit foreign adversaries and state sponsors of terrorism from
purchasing agricultural land in the United States.

S. 5526 would expand reporting requirements under AFIDA to include leases of five years or
more, require foreign persons who transition agricultural land to nonagricultural land to submit
reports to USDA, and amend civil penalty amounts and public reporting from USDA. S. 5526
also would require USDA to conduct annual audits on AFIDA compliance, provide annual
training to state and local personnel, establish an electronic database of land registrations by
foreign owners or leasers, and release an additional report to Congress annually on AFIDA data
and trends.

The bills would amend parts of AFIDA in similar ways. For example, both bills would amend the
civil penalty amounts for AFIDA violations to reflect different types of violations. Both bills also
would require USDA to establish a streamlined database for electronic submission and retention
of AFIDA reports. The timeline to establish the database would differ between the bills, with H.R.
7567 requiring establishment within three years of enactment and S. 5526 within two years. Both
bills would expand USDA’s investigative actions. Specifically, H.R. 7567 would create a new
office at USDA, and S. 5526 would require USDA to conduct an annual compliance audit on

78 H.R. 7567, §12303, states that the reports would be sent to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and

79 The bill would not add USDA as a permanent member agency of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United

## Page 243

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



AFIDA reporting. Both bills would require USDA to submit reports to Congress, though the
required reports would differ in content. For example, H.R. 7567 would require reports relating to
agricultural land transactions for covered foreign countries and state sponsors of terrorism, and S.
5526 would require reports pertaining to general influences of foreign investment (including
national security interests) without specifying covered foreign countries or state sponsors of
terrorism.

Fertilizer

H.R. 7567 does not include provisions that would address fertilizer in Title XII—Miscellaneous.
S. 5526 would require the Secretary of Agriculture to coordinate reports on the domestic and
international crop input market and direct USDA to produce a report on fertilizer production and
use.

S. 5526 would also require the Secretary to establish a program of weekly price reporting for
certain fertilizers and fertilizer products to augment prices currently reported by USDA’s
Agricultural Marketing Service Market News program.80 The bill would require mandatory
weekly price reporting from certain manufacturers and wholesalers and allow for voluntary
weekly price reporting from agricultural cooperatives and retailers.

Title I of both bills include provisions relating to loans for construction of on-farm fertilizer
storage.

Year-Round E15 and RFS Reform

The House Committee on Agriculture and the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and
Forestry both took legislative action to address the year-round sale of E15 and the Renewable
Fuel Standard (RFS) in the 119th Congress. The House addressed these topics in H.R. 1346. The
Senate committee addressed these topics in Section 12501 of S. 5526. E15 is a fuel blend of up to
15% ethanol and 85% gasoline that generally cannot be sold during the summer driving season.81
Both H.R. 1346 and S. 5526 would amend the Clean Air Act (CAA; 42 U.S.C. §7545(f) and 42
U.S.C. §7545(h)) to extend the existing E10 waiver to E15 to allow year-round sales. The RFS
requires U.S. transportation fuel to include a minimum volume of renewable fuel each year.82
Under current law, small refineries are an obligated party to the RFS that may petition for an
exemption from the RFS under certain conditions (e.g., compliance would subject them to
disproportionate economic hardship).83 H.R. 1346 and S. 5526 would amend the CAA to modify
the small refinery exemption process under the RFS, with some differences between the two bills.

U.S. Grain Standards Act Reauthorization

The USGSA, as amended, requires official inspection and weighing of certain grains and oilseeds
sold for export. The USGSA authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to establish official
marketing or quality standards for certain grains and oilseeds, conduct official grain inspections
and weighing services, and supervise official inspections and weighing by authorized state
agencies and official agencies (i.e., private sector entities designated by USDA to conduct official

81 For more information, see CRS Insight IN10979, Year-Round Sale of E15.
82 For more information, see CRS Report R43325, The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS): An Overview.
83 For more information, see CRS Report R46244, The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS): Frequently Asked Questions
About Small Refinery Exemptions (SREs).

## Page 244

The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law



grain inspections and weighing). The federal costs associated with official grain inspections and
weighing are covered by user fees set annually by USDA.84

Although most provisions of the USGSA are permanently authorized, several provisions
authorizing user fee collections and grain inspection advisory committee meetings expired on
September 30, 2025. Congress extended these provisions in the Continuing Appropriations,
Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act,
2026 (P.L. 119-37, Division E, §5001), with certain provisions extended through January 30,
2026, and others extended through September 30, 2026. Historically, Congress has not
reauthorized the USGSA as part of farm bill reauthorization.85

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would reauthorize through September 30, 2033, the USGSA provisions
that expired on January 30, 2026, and the provisions that expired on September 30, 2026. H.R.
7567 and S. 5526 would specify that fees collected must be deposited into a trust fund. H.R. 7567
would amend certain cost calculations for official inspection and weighing services; S. 5526
would maintain current cost calculation formulas.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would authorize the Secretary to allow official agencies (i.e., private
sector entities designated by USDA to conduct official grain inspections and weighing) to
conduct certain official inspections and weighing at export ports. Currently, statute permits
official agencies to conduct official inspections at locations other than export ports. Statute
permits only USDA and authorized state agencies to conduct official inspections and weighing at
export ports.

H.R. 7567 would require grain inspection advisory committee members who have completed two
successive terms to continue serving on completion of their second term until the Secretary
appoints a new member of the committee. S. 5526 would allow advisory committee members to
continue serving on completion of their terms, including their second terms, until the Secretary
appoints a new member of the committee. The Senate committee-reported bill would also require
the Secretary to solicit advisory committee nominations prior to the end of current members’
terms and announce the selection of new committee members within 180 days of the end of the
solicitation period.

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would direct the Secretary to prioritize adoption of improved grain
grading technology. H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 also would exempt costs associated with equipment
and technology development from certain cost calculations. H.R. 7567 would authorize the
Secretary to cooperate with official agencies when conducting research to improve grain grading.
S. 5526 would authorize the Secretary to cooperate with authorized state and official agencies
when conducting research to improve grain grading. H.R. 7567 would require the Secretary to
publish certain data on December 1 of each year, instead of at the discretion of the Secretary, and
make recommendations to improve grain grading and minimize costs for the federal government
and the grain export industry. S. 5526 would require the Secretary—in consultation with
authorized state agencies, official agencies, and the grain industry—to make recommendations to
improve grain grading and minimize costs for the federal government and the grain export
industry.

Other Miscellaneous Provisions

H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would expand fluid milk options that participating schools can offer in the
School Breakfast Program. This change would extend, in statute, the recently enacted changes to
National School Lunch Program milk options (the Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act; P.L. 119-69)
to the School Breakfast Program.86 Both bills would reauthorize the U.S. Drought Monitor. In
addition, the miscellaneous title of H.R. 7567 would amend the USDA farm loan program to
include commercial fishing and fish processing for wild-caught fish and shellfish. S. 5526, in the
credit title, not the miscellaneous title, would amend the farm loan program to include
commercial fishing. Additionally, H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would establish a cost-share grant
program to retrofit tractors with rollover protection structures.

The following provisions were included in H.R. 7567 and not S. 5526. H.R. 7567 would amend
the requirement for USDA to establish a Commission on Farm Transitions (which has not been
established) such that USDA would be required to establish this commission within 60 days of
enactment. The bill would require the Commission on Farm Transitions to expand the required
study to include information on heirs’ property, barriers for historically underserved and women
farmers, and land ownership trends.87 The bill also would extend the commission’s termination
date to September 30, 2031. H.R. 7567 would impose several USDA reporting requirements on
the following topics: USDA personnel, land access and ownership, authorities to address Texas
and Arizona economic losses “due to the failure of Mexico to deliver water,” opportunities for
enhancing pet protections, risk management programs for lamb producers, precision agriculture
satellite connectivity, and certified organic farmers’ access to USDA programs. H.R. 7567 also
would require USDA to provide guidance on the process for importers to obtain information on
imported products that were detained or denied entry under the Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. §§3371-
3378). H.R. 7567 would require USDA to coordinate with the Food and Drug Administration and
U.S. Customs and Border Protection to create a definition of honey and require USDA to
establish specific testing standards for honey.

The following provisions were included in S. 5526 and not H.R. 7567. S. 5526 would define
natural cheese and define a zootechnical animal food substance and deem it a food additive. S.
5526 would amend mandatory country of origin labeling requirements for certain seafood and
beef commodities for certain retail establishments. S. 5526 also would require USDA to study
expanding seafood processing capacity. S. 5526 includes a provision that would establish a
Commission on Rural Maternal Health. The commission would be tasked with studying issues
impacting rural maternal health, such as access to and availability of providers and services and
best practices to reduce adverse maternal health outcomes in rural areas.
